title: Lesson 13: Security and Credentials: Secrets, Least Privilege, and Keeping the Client Safe
description: Handling credentials so they never leak, granting the agent only the least access the work needs, and building guardrails so a mistake or a malicious input cannot become a breach.

questions.question: What makes a piece of data a secret?
options: Its length and the mix of unusual characters that appear inside it
Whether it is stored inside a file that ends in the env extension
The fact that the client specifically asked you to keep the value private
The access it unlocks, no matter how short or unremarkable it looks
questions.explanation: A secret is defined by the access it unlocks, not by its appearance, so a short token that reaches customer records is treated with full care.

questions.question: Why must least privilege be enforced by guardrails rather than by the agent behaving carefully?
options: Because a careful agent runs faster than one that has to ask permission for each action
Because a guardrail refuses on its own when care fails, as with a hostile input
Because guardrails make the agent's own output more accurate and more complete
Because a client cannot observe what the agent does without enforced limits in place
questions.explanation: Guardrails are mechanisms that refuse; they hold when the agent is careless or a hostile input steers it, which is exactly when carefulness fails.

questions.question: What is the correct default for dangerous commands in unattended scheduled work?
options: Approve them automatically so that the recurring job never stalls partway through
Let the agent decide for itself whether each individual command is safe to run
Deny them, so the job must find a safe path or fail in a way that is visible
Approve them only after the job has already run successfully several times
questions.explanation: Unattended work defaults to denying dangerous commands, because a failure you can see is safer than a destructive command that no one approved.
